title: Cross-Time Directional Selection in Diffusion Sampling

paper.title: Cross-Time Directional Selection in Diffusion Sampling
paper.abstract:
Abstract How strongly do the remaining diffusion-sampling steps amplify a perturbation at a late latent state? Standard measurements answer this question with newly sampled isotropic noise, even though perturbations encountered during sampling have already been transformed by earlier steps. We compare these two cases directly. For each trajectory, we transport a centered perturbation from an earlier step to a late state, then replay its direction at the same magnitude as a newly sampled isotropic perturbation; both then undergo the same remaining
updates. Across the samplers we study, median paired shaped-to-fresh angular-gain ratios range from 1.14 1.14 to 2.35 2.35 . Shaped angular gain exceeds its matched
fresh counterpart in every trajectory in the original main cohorts. The same pattern appears when endpoint change is measured by latent RMS. The effect also appears in perceptual feature representations: earlier-sampling directions cause larger feature
changes at the endpoint, even when the corresponding pixel-space change is comparable. Permuting shaped directions across trajectories weakens the effect, including within class, indicating that the advantage depends on alignment with the receiving trajectory as well as on shared directional structure.

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: Perturbation tests estimate how an error during diffusion sampling changes the final sample. The result depends on when the error enters the trajectory, its magnitude, and its direction. A newly sampled Gaussian perturbation is isotropic, whereas an error carried forward from an earlier step has been transformed by the intervening updates. Whether these two kinds of perturbation have the same effect on the final sample is an empirical question. Prior work has identified distinct temporal regimes in diffusion, regularity in sampling paths, the accumulation of errors, and anisotropic score geometry ( Biroli et al., 2024 ; Chen et al., 2024 ; Li and van der Schaar, 2024 ; Ventura et al., 2025 ) . Together, these findings raise a more specific question: do early sampling steps produce perturbation directions that the remaining sampler amplifies particularly strongly? Averaging over newly sampled probes cannot resolve this question, because it does not test directions generated by the trajectory itself. Likewise, the alignment of a trajectory with its endpoint describes the path taken by one sample, rather than the sampler’s response to nearby states. We compare newly sampled perturbations with directions produced upstream, while holding the remaining updates fixed. Starting from a Gaussian direction, we perturb an earlier state in opposite directions and propagate both perturbed trajectories to a common late boundary. Their centered difference defines the upstream-shaped direction, which we normalize and replay around the unperturbed boundary state. The fresh probe uses the original Gaussian direction at the same RMS magnitude. This construction holds the perturbation size and late reference state fixed, leaving the direction produced by upstream transport as the only difference between the two probes. Across the three samplers, upstream-shaped directions have median paired angular gains 1.14 1.14 – 2.35 2.35 times those of matched fresh probes. Shaped angular gain exceeds fresh gain in every trajectory in the original main cohorts. The ordering persists over a shorter late window and when measured by latent-RMS gain. Repeating the SiT comparison over an eightfold range of small replay magnitudes leaves the median paired ratio essentially unchanged. At equal replay magnitude around the endpoint state, early-shaped directions also induce larger changes in two independent image-feature representations. We then test whether the effect transfers across trajectories by replaying shaped directions on a different trajectory. In new SiT and DiT cohorts, a trajectory responds more strongly to its own shaped direction than to a direction taken from another trajectory, even when both samples share a class label. Because this permutation preserves the population of shaped directions while breaking their pairing with the late state, the result shows that shared directional anisotropy alone cannot explain the effect. We introduce a matched replay measurement for cross-time directional selection in diffusion sampling. It isolates the relation between directions shaped by early updates and the sensitivity of later updates, beyond anisotropy measured at a single state. The matched and donor comparisons show both that early updates shape directions that are preferentially transmitted later and that this preference depends on their alignment with the receiving trajectory. We also examine endpoint image-feature changes and report trajectory geometry and fresh-probe crossover timing in Appendix C . Figure 1: Matched replay tests cross-time directional selection. (A) We transport a perturbation from a a to b b to obtain an upstream-shaped direction. We then replay this direction and a fresh Gaussian direction at equal RMS magnitude around the same unperturbed late state z b z_{b} , and pass both through the same remaining updates. (B) Median paired shaped-to-fresh endpoint angular-gain ratios, shown for each sampler and source time.

sections.heading: Temporal structure and trajectory geometry.
sections.text: Diffusion sampling has distinct temporal regimes, including symmetry breaking, speciation, and feature-decision windows ( Raya and Ambrogioni, 2023 ; Biroli et al., 2024 ; Sclocchi et al., 2024 ; Li and Chen, 2024 ) . Sampling paths also exhibit regular geometric structure ( Chen et al., 2024 ) , while derivatives of normalized score or update directions identify time ranges that are particularly sensitive to intervention ( Sakamoto and Sakamoto, 2026 ) . These studies characterize how sampling changes over time; our alignment and angular-speed measurements situate the matched perturbation experiments within that temporal structure.

sections.heading: Error propagation and contraction.
sections.text: Local errors can accumulate, composed flow maps can amplify them, and stepwise contraction guarantees can fail ( Li and van der Schaar, 2024 ; Gao et al., 2026 ; Li and Zeng, 2026 ) . Spatial integration errors have also been tracked through the remaining sampler ( Yin, 2026 ) . These results motivate asking whether the downstream response also depends on the direction of the error. We hold the late state, perturbation magnitude, and remaining updates fixed, then compare fresh isotropic directions with directions shaped by earlier sampling steps.

sections.heading: Directional geometry.
sections.text: Low-noise scores approximate normal directions to the data manifold ( Stanczuk et al., 2023 ) , and score-Jacobian spectra distinguish tangent and normal subspaces across generative phases ( Ventura et al., 2025 ) . These results suggest that directional anisotropy may shape how perturbations propagate. Our experiment compares fresh and upstream-shaped directions under the same remaining updates. By transporting directions across time and exchanging them between trajectories, we test whether the resulting directional preference persists downstream and depends on the receiving state.

sections.heading: Sampling and aggregation.
sections.text: For each model, we sample 1,024 independently seeded trajectories with labels cycling through the 1,000 ImageNet classes (24 classes occur twice and the remainder once). We evaluate two Gaussian axes per trajectory, with the positive and negative branches forming one symmetric measurement. For trajectory n n , we take the median across axes separately for shaped and fresh gains, yielding g n ( a ) g_{n}^{(a)} and g n f g_{n}^{f} , and compute the paired ratio g n ( a ) / g n f g_{n}^{(a)}/g_{n}^{f} . We report the median of these paired ratios across trajectories, separately for each model. This differs from the ratio of marginal median gains.

sections.heading: Donor replay.
sections.text: We run donor replay on new 256-trajectory cohorts for SiT and DiT, with four seeds for each of 64 ImageNet classes. For every source condition, we construct two within-class and two across-class permutations of shaped directions and replay each donor direction around its recipient’s late state. The permutation preserves the full shaped-direction ensemble while changing its pairing with the recipient state. Class conditioning, replay magnitude, late boundary, and remaining updates are held fixed. We summarize donor-to-fresh and own-to-donor paired gain ratios using the aggregation above.

sections.heading: 3.4 Endpoint representation sensitivity
sections.text: The gain experiment measures how perturbations propagate through the late sampler. A second experiment asks whether the resulting directions differ in their decoded effect once their magnitude is equalized. For each fresh or shaped direction at T T , we normalize the centered branch displacement to unit RMS and replay it at radius 0.00125 ​ RMS ⁡ ( z T ) 0.00125\operatorname{RMS}(z_{T}) around the unperturbed endpoint. No diffusion updates follow. We decode the plus and minus replay states with the same VAE and use half their pixel-RMS distance and half their feature-space distance as responses. We use L2-normalized DINOv2 CLS tokens and mean-pooled patch tokens ( Oquab et al., 2023 ) , as well as ResNet-50 features ( He et al., 2016 ) . For each response H H , we compute the shaped-to-fresh ratio for each probe axis, take the geometric mean of the two axis-wise ratios within each trajectory, and report the median of these trajectory-level ratios. This aggregation differs from the gain comparison above, which first takes the median gain across axes separately for shaped and fresh probes and then forms their ratio within each trajectory. We also report the fraction of axis pairs with a larger shaped response; these pairs share trajectories and are descriptive rather than independent observations. Together, the pixel and feature responses measure the effect of equal-magnitude endpoint perturbations on decoded images and image representations. We run this endpoint experiment on 256 SiT trajectories.

sections.heading: 4 Results
sections.text: Our main result compares upstream-shaped and fresh directions at the same late state. We report the size of this effect, its robustness checks, and the donor control. Finally, endpoint replay tests whether equal-magnitude directions produce different changes in decoded image features. Native trajectory geometry and fresh-probe crossover timing are reported in Appendix C.

sections.heading: 4.1 Late updates preferentially transmit upstream-shaped directions
sections.text: At the late boundary, fresh and upstream-shaped perturbations are injected at the same RMS magnitude around the same unperturbed state and undergo the same remaining updates. The ordering is already present over the four-update window from the replay boundary, where median shaped-to-fresh ratios range from 1.079 to 1.552. The effect is largest for early source times. Fresh probes have median angular gain below one in all three models, whereas directions shaped from step 5 have median gain above one. The advantage declines as the source approaches the replay boundary. At step 35, shaped probes also contract in SiT and LightningDiT, but less than their matched fresh probes. Thus the late map responds more strongly to upstream-shaped directions whether it expands or contracts the perturbation. The paired contrast is stable across the tested replay radii. In the SiT audit, an eight-fold change in replay radius alters the median paired ratio by at most 0.0004 (supplementary Figure 2 ). For example, SiT directions shaped from step 35 have median angular gain 0.927 and median RMS gain 1.083; for LightningDiT directions shaped from step 20, the corresponding values are 0.908 and 1.084. The robust result is stronger relative transmission of shaped directions. In these cases, angular separation contracts while latent-space distance expands.

sections.heading: 4.2 The advantage depends on pairing directions with their trajectory
sections.text: We evaluate donor replay on new 256-trajectory cohorts for SiT and DiT. Shaped directions are reassigned to recipient trajectories either within class or across classes, while the recipient state, conditioning, replay magnitude, and remaining updates remain fixed. At source step 5, own shaped directions have median gain ratios of 1.509 in SiT and 2.353 in DiT relative to fresh probes. Reassigned donor directions retain a substantially smaller advantage: donor-to-fresh ratios are 1.059 and 1.191 for within-class assignments, and 1.057 and 1.192 for across-class assignments. Direct own-to-donor ratios are 1.413 and 2.004 within class, and 1.410 and 2.001 across classes. The own-direction advantage remains at sources 20 and 35 (Appendix B ). Reassigning directions preserves their population while substantially reducing their advantage. The result therefore depends on how a shaped direction aligns with its recipient trajectory, beyond shared or class-level directional structure. This dependence on direction–trajectory pairing is also compatible with trajectory-specific correlations between upstream and downstream Jacobians in the small-perturbation regime.

sections.heading: 4.3 Early-shaped directions induce larger endpoint feature responses
sections.text: The matched-gain result shows that upstream-shaped directions propagate more strongly through the late sampler. We next ask whether equal-magnitude replay of these directions also produces different decoded responses. In SiT, directions shaped from step 5 produce larger DINOv2 and ResNet-50 feature responses than their paired fresh directions, while the pixel-RMS response ratio remains near one (Table 2 ; supplementary Figure 3 ). The feature-space advantage weakens at source step 20 and is absent or nearly absent at step 35. Because every direction is replayed at the same RMS magnitude around the same endpoint state, inherited transport magnitude cannot explain this contrast. The effect therefore extends from latent-space propagation to decoded image-feature representations.

sections.heading: 5 Discussion and Limitations
sections.text: The matched experiment separates the response to newly drawn isotropic directions from the response to directions produced by earlier updates. With the late state and replay magnitude held fixed, these direction populations receive different downstream gain. Fresh-probe averages therefore describe the response to a particular probe population when assessing deviations carried through sampling. The Gaussian probes serve as controlled interventions. Their relation to solver, quantization, and caching error distributions is not evaluated in the reported experiments.

sections.heading: Interpretation of the contrast.
sections.text: In the small-perturbation regime, upstream transport approximately transforms a probe by J a : b J_{a:b} , while the remaining updates act through J b : c J_{b:c} . Correlations between the sensitive directions of these trajectory-dependent maps could therefore account for the shaped-direction advantage. The stability of the paired ratio over the tested small-radius range is consistent with this interpretation. Donor reassignment shows that pairing with the recipient trajectory matters, but remains compatible with the same linear account. The reported experiments characterize this directional preference without isolating its underlying mechanism.

sections.heading: Measurement limits.
sections.text: The paired summaries use two probe axes per trajectory and characterize typical directional response rather than local spectra or worst-case gain. They concern discrete samplers at fixed step counts. Solver choice, stochastic sampling, guidance scale, and broader model families define the current scope. Normalized update index aligns plotting positions across models, while their noise schedules, latent representations, and training recipes differ.

sections.heading: Endpoint and timing interpretations.
sections.text: The endpoint experiment is a SiT study with a fixed VAE and feature encoders. It measures representation response under equal-magnitude replay rather than human-perceptual fidelity. The timing association describes co-variation across trajectories; it does not identify the cause of the matched contrast. These results matter for evaluating sampler approximations. A late window can attenuate fresh perturbations while continuing to transmit directions arriving from earlier updates. Evaluations of reduced precision or cached computation therefore need perturbations that reflect this upstream transport. Matched replay controls their arrival magnitude, and pairing it with measured approximation residuals would test consequences for endpoint fidelity and sample quality.

sections.heading: 6 Conclusion
sections.text: Across the three samplers, directions shaped by earlier updates receive greater late-map gain than fresh isotropic directions replayed at the same state and RMS magnitude. The shaped-over-fresh ordering appears in both angular and latent-RMS measurements, while the location of unit gain depends on the metric. In SiT and DiT, reassigning shaped directions to other trajectories substantially reduces their advantage, including within class, showing that direction–trajectory pairing matters. A stability measurement is defined jointly by its time window and perturbation population. Tracking directions through the preceding sampler reveals a late response that fresh probes alone do not capture, and shows that much of the advantage is tied to the trajectory on which those directions were formed.

sections.heading: 7 Impact Statement
sections.text: This work studies the sampling dynamics of existing image generators and does not introduce a new generation or editing capability. The diagnostic itself requires additional perturbed sampling branches. If used to guide approximate sampling or training changes, it could reduce generation cost while inheriting the risks of the underlying image generator. Such use should be evaluated for image quality, diversity, and bias.

sections.heading: C.1 Timing of angular motion and fresh-probe contraction
sections.text: We examine how the full-horizon angular gain of fresh probes changes as their injection time moves later in sampling, and compare the transition to contraction with the timing of angular motion along the unperturbed trajectory. We evaluate fresh probes injected at steps { 4 , 8 , 12 , 16 , 20 , 24 , 28 , 32 , 36 , 40 , 44 } \{4,8,12,16,20,24,28,32,36,40,44\} on 256 SiT trajectories. For each trajectory, the crossover is the first injection whose median gain across axes falls below one and remains below one at all later tested injections. We estimate its location by linearly interpolating log gain around the crossing and normalize it by 49; persistence is assessed on the tested injection grid. In this cohort, median crossover progress is 0.451 and median angular-speed peak progress is 0.643. The two quantities have Spearman correlation ρ = 0.622 \rho=0.622 across trajectories; the axis-specific correlations are 0.626 and 0.555. Trajectories with later angular-speed peaks also tend to have later fresh-probe crossovers, while contraction typically begins before peak angular motion. Thus, angular contraction of nearby perturbations can coexist with substantial angular motion of the underlying trajectory. This timing association is descriptive and does not establish a mechanism for the shaped-to-fresh gain contrast. These timing measurements use a separate 256-trajectory SiT cohort from the 1,024-trajectory cohorts used to characterize geometry below. Figure 4: Timing association in SiT. sections.heading: C.2 Trajectory geometry and tangential-speed validation
sections.text: We characterize unperturbed trajectory geometry on 1,024 trajectories per model using the measurements defined in Section 3.1. Alignment with the endpoint rises smoothly in all three models (Figure 5 A). Meanwhile, angular speed rises to a model-specific maximum before falling (Figure 5 B). The median position of the trajectory-level angular-speed peak is normalized progress 0.622 for SiT, 0.870 for DiT, and 0.500 for LightningDiT. Thus, a state can become increasingly aligned with its endpoint while continuing to rotate substantially. The relative tangential-speed control closely tracks the angular-speed profile. Their median curves differ by at most 0.019 for SiT, 0.018 for DiT, and 0.024 for LightningDiT, and their median trajectory-level peak-step difference is zero in every model. Absolute tangential motion also peaks near the angular maximum. These controls support that the angular-speed peak reflects increased sideways motion, rather than merely normalization by a changing latent norm. Report Issue Back to Abstract Download PDF Contents Reading mode Colour theme License: CC BY 4.0 arXiv:2610.05199v1 [cs.LG] 04 Oct 2026 \workshoptitle AI for Stochastic Dynamics Cross-Time Directional Selection in Diffusion Sampling Dhia Naouali Affiliation: Independent Researcher Email: dhia12naouali@gmail.com Abstract How strongly do the remaining diffusion-sampling steps amplify a perturbation at a late latent state? Standard measurements answer this question with newly sampled isotropic noise, even though perturbations encountered during sampling have already been transformed by earlier steps. We compare these two cases directly. For each trajectory, we transport a centered perturbation from an earlier step to a late state, then replay its direction at the same magnitude as a newly sampled isotropic perturbation; both then undergo the same remaining updates. Across the samplers we study, median paired shaped-to-fresh angular-gain ratios range from 1.14 1.14 to 2.35 2.35 . Shaped angular gain exceeds its matched fresh counterpart in every trajectory in the original main cohorts. The same pattern appears when endpoint change is measured by latent RMS. The effect also appears in perceptual feature representations: earlier-sampling directions cause larger feature changes at the endpoint, even when the corresponding pixel-space change is comparable. Permuting shaped directions across trajectories weakens the effect, including within class, indicating that the advantage depends on alignment with the receiving trajectory as well as on shared directional structure. 1 Introduction Perturbation tests estimate how an error during diffusion sampling changes the final sample. The result depends on when the error enters the trajectory, its magnitude, and its direction. A newly sampled Gaussian perturbation is isotropic, whereas an error carried forward from an earlier step has been transformed by the intervening updates. Whether these two kinds of perturbation have the same effect on the final sample is an empirical question. Prior work has identified distinct temporal regimes in diffusion, regularity in sampling paths, the accumulation of errors, and anisotropic score geometry ( Biroli et al., 2024 ; Chen et al., 2024 ; Li and van der Schaar, 2024 ; Ventura et al., 2025 ) . Together, these findings raise a more specific question: do early sampling steps produce perturbation directions that the remaining sampler amplifies particularly strongly? Averaging over newly sampled probes cannot resolve this question, because it does not test directions generated by the trajectory itself. Likewise, the alignment of a trajectory with its endpoint describes the path taken by one sample, rather than the sampler’s response to nearby states. We compare newly sampled perturbations with directions produced upstream, while holding the remaining updates fixed. Starting from a Gaussian direction, we perturb an earlier state in opposite directions and propagate both perturbed trajectories to a common late boundary. Their centered difference defines the upstream-shaped direction, which we normalize and replay around the unperturbed boundary state. The fresh probe uses the original Gaussian direction at the same RMS magnitude. This construction holds the perturbation size and late reference state fixed, leaving the direction produced by upstream transport as the only difference between the two probes. Across the three samplers, upstream-shaped directions have median paired angular gains 1.14 1.14 – 2.35 2.35 times those of matched fresh probes. Shaped angular gain exceeds fresh gain in every trajectory in the original main cohorts. The ordering persists over a shorter late window and when measured by latent-RMS gain. Repeating the SiT comparison over an eightfold range of small replay magnitudes leaves the median paired ratio essentially unchanged. At equal replay magnitude around the endpoint state, early-shaped directions also induce larger changes in two independent image-feature representations. We then test whether the effect transfers across trajectories by replaying shaped directions on a different trajectory. In new SiT and DiT cohorts, a trajectory responds more strongly to its own shaped direction than to a direction taken from another trajectory, even when both samples share a class label. Because this permutation preserves the population of shaped directions while breaking their pairing with the late state, the result shows that shared directional anisotropy alone cannot explain the effect. We introduce a matched replay measurement for cross-time directional selection in diffusion sampling. It isolates the relation between directions shaped by early updates and the sensitivity of later updates, beyond anisotropy measured at a single state. The matched and donor comparisons show both that early updates shape directions that are preferentially transmitted later and that this preference depends on their alignment with the receiving trajectory. We also examine endpoint image-feature changes and report trajectory geometry and fresh-probe crossover timing in Appendix C . Figure 1: Matched replay tests cross-time directional selection. (A) We transport a perturbation from a a to b b to obtain an upstream-shaped direction. We then replay this direction and a fresh Gaussian direction at equal RMS magnitude around the same unperturbed late state z b z_{b} , and pass both through the same remaining updates. (B) Median paired shaped-to-fresh endpoint angular-gain ratios, shown for each sampler and source time. 2 Related Work Temporal structure and trajectory geometry. Diffusion sampling has distinct temporal regimes, including symmetry breaking, speciation, and feature-decision windows ( Raya and Ambrogioni, 2023 ; Biroli et al., 2024 ; Sclocchi et al., 2024 ; Li and Chen, 2024 ) . Sampling paths also exhibit regular geometric structure ( Chen et al., 2024 ) , while derivatives of normalized score or update directions identify time ranges that are particularly sensitive to intervention ( Sakamoto and Sakamoto, 2026 ) . These studies characterize how sampling changes over time; our alignment and angular-speed measurements situate the matched perturbation experiments within that temporal structure. Error propagation and contraction. Local errors can accumulate, composed flow maps can amplify them, and stepwise contraction guarantees can fail ( Li and van der Schaar, 2024 ; Gao et al., 2026 ; Li and Zeng, 2026 ) . Spatial integration errors have also been tracked through the remaining sampler ( Yin, 2026 ) . These results motivate asking whether the downstream response also depends on the direction of the error. We hold the late state, perturbation magnitude, and remaining updates fixed, then compare fresh isotropic directions with directions shaped by earlier sampling steps. Directional geometry. Low-noise scores approximate normal directions to the data manifold ( Stanczuk et al., 2023 ) , and score-Jacobian spectra distinguish tangent and normal subspaces across generative phases ( Ventura et al., 2025 ) . These results suggest that directional anisotropy may shape how perturbations propagate. Our experiment compares fresh and upstream-shaped directions under the same remaining updates. By transporting directions across time and exchanging them between trajectories, we test whether the resulting directional preference persists downstream and depends on the receiving state. 3 Methods 3.1 Setting and trajectory geometry We analyze deterministic sampling trajectories from pretrained SiT-XL/2 ( Ma et al., 2024 ) , DiT-XL/2 ( Peebles and Xie, 2023 ) , and LightningDiT-XL/1 ( Yao et al., 2025 ) , all at ImageNet 256 × 256 256\times 256 resolution with guidance scale 1. The paired RMS comparison determines whether the directional ordering also appears in latent-space distance. Sampling and aggregation. For each model, we sample 1,024 independently seeded trajectories with labels cycling through the 1,000 ImageNet classes (24 classes occur twice and the remainder once). We evaluate two Gaussian axes per trajectory, with the positive and negative branches forming one symmetric measurement. For trajectory n n , we take the median across axes separately for shaped and fresh gains, yielding g n ( a ) g_{n}^{(a)} and g n f g_{n}^{f} , and compute the paired ratio g n ( a ) / g n f g_{n}^{(a)}/g_{n}^{f} . We report the median of these paired ratios across trajectories, separately for each model. This differs from the ratio of marginal median gains. Donor replay. We run donor replay on new 256-trajectory cohorts for SiT and DiT, with four seeds for each of 64 ImageNet classes. For every source condition, we construct two within-class and two across-class permutations of shaped directions and replay each donor direction around its recipient’s late state. The permutation preserves the full shaped-direction ensemble while changing its pairing with the recipient state. Class conditioning, replay magnitude, late boundary, and remaining updates are held fixed. We summarize donor-to-fresh and own-to-donor paired gain ratios using the aggregation above. 3.4 Endpoint representation sensitivity The gain experiment measures how perturbations propagate through the late sampler. A second experiment asks whether the resulting directions differ in their decoded effect once their magnitude is equalized. For each fresh or shaped direction at T T , we normalize the centered branch displacement to unit RMS and replay it at radius 0.00125 ​ RMS ⁡ ( z T ) 0.00125\operatorname{RMS}(z_{T}) around the unperturbed endpoint. No diffusion updates follow. We decode the plus and minus replay states with the same VAE and use half their pixel-RMS distance and half their feature-space distance as responses. We use L2-normalized DINOv2 CLS tokens and mean-pooled patch tokens ( Oquab et al., 2023 ) , as well as ResNet-50 features ( He et al., 2016 ) . For each response H H , we compute the shaped-to-fresh ratio for each probe axis, take the geometric mean of the two axis-wise ratios within each trajectory, and report the median of these trajectory-level ratios. This aggregation differs from the gain comparison above, which first takes the median gain across axes separately for shaped and fresh probes and then forms their ratio within each trajectory. We also report the fraction of axis pairs with a larger shaped response; these pairs share trajectories and are descriptive rather than independent observations. Together, the pixel and feature responses measure the effect of equal-magnitude endpoint perturbations on decoded images and image representations. We run this endpoint experiment on 256 SiT trajectories. 4 Results Our main result compares upstream-shaped and fresh directions at the same late state. We report the size of this effect, its robustness checks, and the donor control. Finally, endpoint replay tests whether equal-magnitude directions produce different changes in decoded image features. Native trajectory geometry and fresh-probe crossover timing are reported in Appendix C. 4.1 Late updates preferentially transmit upstream-shaped directions At the late boundary, fresh and upstream-shaped perturbations are injected at the same RMS magnitude around the same unperturbed state and undergo the same remaining updates. Across every model and source time, the upstream-shaped direction produces greater endpoint angular gain (Figure 1 ; Table 1 ). Table 1: Median endpoint angular gain. The ordering is already present over the four-update window from the replay boundary, where median shaped-to-fresh ratios range from 1.079 to 1.552. The effect is largest for early source times. Fresh probes have median angular gain below one in all three models, whereas directions shaped from step 5 have median gain above one. The advantage declines as the source approaches the replay boundary. At step 35, shaped probes also contract in SiT and LightningDiT, but less than their matched fresh probes. Thus the late map responds more strongly to upstream-shaped directions whether it expands or contracts the perturbation. The paired contrast is stable across the tested replay radii. In the SiT audit, an eight-fold change in replay radius alters the median paired ratio by at most 0.0004 (supplementary Figure 2 ). A separate source-radius audit changes the median paired angular-gain ratio by less than 0.009 % 0.009\% in every model (Appendix B ). Latent-RMS gain preserves the shaped-over-fresh ordering, although whether an individual gain lies above or below one can depend on the metric. For example, SiT directions shaped from step 35 have median angular gain 0.927 and median RMS gain 1.083; for LightningDiT directions shaped from step 20, the corresponding values are 0.908 and 1.084. The robust result is stronger relative transmission of shaped directions. In these cases, angular separation contracts while latent-space distance expands. 4.2 The advantage depends on pairing directions with their trajectory We evaluate donor replay on new 256-trajectory cohorts for SiT and DiT. Shaped directions are reassigned to recipient trajectories either within class or across classes, while the recipient state, conditioning, replay magnitude, and remaining updates remain fixed. At source step 5, own shaped directions have median gain ratios of 1.509 in SiT and 2.353 in DiT relative to fresh probes. Reassigned donor directions retain a substantially smaller advantage: donor-to-fresh ratios are 1.059 and 1.191 for within-class assignments, and 1.057 and 1.192 for across-class assignments. Direct own-to-donor ratios are 1.413 and 2.004 within class, and 1.410 and 2.001 across classes. The own-direction advantage remains at sources 20 and 35 (Appendix B ). Reassigning directions preserves their population while substantially reducing their advantage. The result therefore depends on how a shaped direction aligns with its recipient trajectory, beyond shared or class-level directional structure. This dependence on direction–trajectory pairing is also compatible with trajectory-specific correlations between upstream and downstream Jacobians in the small-perturbation regime. 4.3 Early-shaped directions induce larger endpoint feature responses The matched-gain result shows that upstream-shaped directions propagate more strongly through the late sampler. We next ask whether equal-magnitude replay of these directions also produces different decoded responses. In SiT, directions shaped from step 5 produce larger DINOv2 and ResNet-50 feature responses than their paired fresh directions, while the pixel-RMS response ratio remains near one (Table 2 ; supplementary Figure 3 ). The feature-space advantage weakens at source step 20 and is absent or nearly absent at step 35. Because every direction is replayed at the same RMS magnitude around the same endpoint state, inherited transport magnitude cannot explain this contrast. The effect therefore extends from latent-space propagation to decoded image-feature representations. 5 Discussion and Limitations The matched experiment separates the response to newly drawn isotropic directions from the response to directions produced by earlier updates. With the late state and replay magnitude held fixed, these direction populations receive different downstream gain. Fresh-probe averages therefore describe the response to a particular probe population when assessing deviations carried through sampling. The Gaussian probes serve as controlled interventions. Their relation to solver, quantization, and caching error distributions is not evaluated in the reported experiments. Interpretation of the contrast. In the small-perturbation regime, upstream transport approximately transforms a probe by J a : b J_{a:b} , while the remaining updates act through J b : c J_{b:c} . Correlations between the sensitive directions of these trajectory-dependent maps could therefore account for the shaped-direction advantage. The stability of the paired ratio over the tested small-radius range is consistent with this interpretation. Donor reassignment shows that pairing with the recipient trajectory matters, but remains compatible with the same linear account. The reported experiments characterize this directional preference without isolating its underlying mechanism. Measurement limits. The paired summaries use two probe axes per trajectory and characterize typical directional response rather than local spectra or worst-case gain. They concern discrete samplers at fixed step counts. Solver choice, stochastic sampling, guidance scale, and broader model families define the current scope. Normalized update index aligns plotting positions across models, while their noise schedules, latent representations, and training recipes differ. Endpoint and timing interpretations. The endpoint experiment is a SiT study with a fixed VAE and feature encoders. It measures representation response under equal-magnitude replay rather than human-perceptual fidelity. The timing association describes co-variation across trajectories; it does not identify the cause of the matched contrast. These results matter for evaluating sampler approximations. A late window can attenuate fresh perturbations while continuing to transmit directions arriving from earlier updates. Evaluations of reduced precision or cached computation therefore need perturbations that reflect this upstream transport. Matched replay controls their arrival magnitude, and pairing it with measured approximation residuals would test consequences for endpoint fidelity and sample quality. 6 Conclusion Across the three samplers, directions shaped by earlier updates receive greater late-map gain than fresh isotropic directions replayed at the same state and RMS magnitude. The shaped-over-fresh ordering appears in both angular and latent-RMS measurements, while the location of unit gain depends on the metric. In SiT and DiT, reassigning shaped directions to other trajectories substantially reduces their advantage, including within class, showing that direction–trajectory pairing matters. A stability measurement is defined jointly by its time window and perturbation population. Tracking directions through the preceding sampler reveals a late response that fresh probes alone do not capture, and shows that much of the advantage is tied to the trajectory on which those directions were formed. 7 Impact Statement This work studies the sampling dynamics of existing image generators and does not introduce a new generation or editing capability. The diagnostic itself requires additional perturbed sampling branches. If used to guide approximate sampling or training changes, it could reduce generation cost while inheriting the risks of the underlying image generator. C.1 Timing of angular motion and fresh-probe contraction We examine how the full-horizon angular gain of fresh probes changes as their injection time moves later in sampling, and compare the transition to contraction with the timing of angular motion along the unperturbed trajectory. We evaluate fresh probes injected at steps { 4 , 8 , 12 , 16 , 20 , 24 , 28 , 32 , 36 , 40 , 44 } \{4,8,12,16,20,24,28,32,36,40,44\} on 256 SiT trajectories. For each trajectory, the crossover is the first injection whose median gain across axes falls below one and remains below one at all later tested injections. We estimate its location by linearly interpolating log gain around the crossing and normalize it by 49; persistence is assessed on the tested injection grid. In this cohort, median crossover progress is 0.451 and median angular-speed peak progress is 0.643. The two quantities have Spearman correlation ρ = 0.622 \rho=0.622 across trajectories; the axis-specific correlations are 0.626 and 0.555. Trajectories with later angular-speed peaks also tend to have later fresh-probe crossovers, while contraction typically begins before peak angular motion. Thus, angular contraction of nearby perturbations can coexist with substantial angular motion of the underlying trajectory. This timing association is descriptive and does not establish a mechanism for the shaped-to-fresh gain contrast. C.2 Trajectory geometry and tangential-speed validation We characterize unperturbed trajectory geometry on 1,024 trajectories per model using the measurements defined in Section 3.1. Alignment with the endpoint rises smoothly in all three models (Figure 5 A). Meanwhile, angular speed rises to a model-specific maximum before falling (Figure 5 B). The median position of the trajectory-level angular-speed peak is normalized progress 0.622 for SiT, 0.870 for DiT, and 0.500 for LightningDiT. Thus, a state can become increasingly aligned with its endpoint while continuing to rotate substantially. The relative tangential-speed control closely tracks the angular-speed profile. Their median curves differ by at most 0.019 for SiT, 0.018 for DiT, and 0.024 for LightningDiT, and their median trajectory-level peak-step difference is zero in every model. Absolute tangential motion also peaks near the angular maximum. These controls support that the angular-speed peak reflects increased sideways motion, rather than merely normalization by a changing latent norm.
